scenarios.title: Scenario 3 — Multi-Agent Research System
scenarios.domains: D1 Agentic Architecture · D2 Tool Design & MCP · D5 Context & Reliability
scenarios.brief: A market-intelligence firm runs a research system on the Claude Agent SDK. A coordinator delegates through the Task tool to six subagents: web search, filings analysis, document analysis, synthesis, fact-check and report generation. Each subagent runs in its own context. Reports run to about 4,000 words with inline citations, cost about $4.10 per run and take 9–16 minutes.

scenarios.title: Scenario 4 — Developer Productivity with Claude
scenarios.domains: D2 Tool Design & MCP · D1 Agentic Architecture · D3 Claude Code Configuration
scenarios.brief: An engineer works in Claude Code on a 400,000-line Python and TypeScript order service, with the built-in tools plus MCP servers for GitHub, Jira and a newly added Sentry server that exposes production error groups. The repository also holds the Terraform for production. The engineer is onboarding two joiners, so shared setup must work for them on clone. Current task: find why one error group spiked after Tuesday's deploy.

questions.question: To cut cost on small requests, the team built a second coordinator, quick-brief, from the original's configuration. Its prompt was edited to describe when to hand work to the filings-analysis and fact-check subagents, and its tool list was written fresh as Read, WebSearch and WebFetch. In trials, quick-brief returns reasonable reports, but filings figures come from web pages and checks happen inline; traces show no output from either subagent. The original coordinator still delegates to both. What is the most likely cause?

options.t: The two subagents' descriptions are too vague for quick-brief's shorter prompt to match a request to either of them.
options.why: Runner-up. Vague descriptions cause missed or wrong delegation, and they would be the first suspect if some subagents ran and these two did not. Here neither ever runs, and the original coordinator reaches them fine, so selection is not the step that fails.

options.t: The subagents start without the coordinator's history, and with no findings in their prompts they return nothing usable.
options.why: Incorrect. Context isolation is real, but it produces a subagent that runs and returns weak output. The traces show no output at all, meaning neither subagent was started.

options.t: Quick-brief's allowedTools list lacks "Task", and it falls back to doing the work with the tools it holds.
options.why: Correct. Subagents are spawned through the Task tool, and allowedTools must include "Task". A tool list rewritten as Read, WebSearch and WebFetch removes the only way to delegate, so quick-brief does the work itself.

options.t: The prompt presents delegation as optional, and the coordinator favours inline work unless each step names a subagent.
options.why: Incorrect. Goal-style prompts are the recommended style, and a coordinator that can call Task does delegate from them, as the original shows. No wording can start a subagent the coordinator has no tool to spawn.

questions.explanation: Delegation has a hard prerequisite: the coordinator must be able to call the Task tool, so allowedTools must include "Task". When no subagent runs at all, check capability before tuning descriptions or prompt wording.
questions.decider: Quick-brief's tool list was written fresh as Read, WebSearch and WebFetch and neither subagent ever produces output; if Task were present and only some delegations were skipped, vague subagent descriptions would be the likelier cause.

eli5.question: A new coordinator never hands work to its helpers. The clue is: its tool list was written fresh as Read, WebSearch and WebFetch. The question is not how well the helpers are described. It is whether the coordinator can hand work over at all.
eli5.answer: Picture a manager with staff but no way to send them tasks. However clear the job descriptions, nothing gets delegated, so the manager does it all alone. A coordinator hands out work through the Task tool, and that tool must be in its allowedTools. Quick-brief's list left it out. Rule: if no subagent ever runs, check that the coordinator can call Task.
options: Runner-up. Unclear helper descriptions (AgentDefinition descriptions) cause missed hand-offs. This would win if some helpers ran and only these two were skipped.
Helpers do start with a blank memory (isolated context). That gives weak answers, not no answers. These helpers never started.
Correct. Without Task in its tool list, quick-brief has no way to start a subagent.
Prompt wording shapes when to delegate. It cannot give the coordinator a tool it does not have.

deep.premise: It is tempting to treat delegation as a prompt-and-description problem: if the coordinator does not delegate, it must not recognise when to. That is only true once the coordinator can delegate. Starting a subagent is itself a tool call, the Task tool. A coordinator whose allowedTools lacks it has nothing to call, however good its prompt.

questions.question: Finance wants the per-run cost down. A trace review finds that in 22% of runs the web-search and filings-analysis subagents both fetch and summarise the same investor presentations, adding about $0.70 each time. Those runs answer broad questions, such as how five listed competitors are positioning on price, and their reports cite material from both subagents. The coordinator spawns the two in parallel with the instructions 'research the competitive landscape' and 'analyse company disclosures'. Which change most directly removes the duplicated work?

options.t: Have the coordinator judge each question's breadth and send disclosure-centred questions to the filings subagent alone.
options.why: Runner-up. Choosing subagents by what a question needs is right when one subagent could answer alone. These questions are broad and their reports draw on both subagents, so dropping one loses coverage rather than duplication.

options.t: Give each subagent named source classes and exclusions: filings and investor decks to one, press coverage to the other.
options.why: Correct. The overlap comes from two remits that both cover company presentations. Partitioning sources explicitly in each delegation makes the territories disjoint, so the duplicate fetches stop while both subagents still run.

options.t: Return each finding with its URL in a separate metadata field and have the coordinator drop repeated URLs before synthesis.
options.why: Incorrect. Separating content from metadata is good practice, and de-duplicating would tidy the input to synthesis. But the duplicate fetching and summarising has already been paid for by then, so the cost stays.

options.t: Start filings analysis after web search completes and include the search subagent's complete findings in its prompt.
options.why: Incorrect. Passing complete prior findings forward is right when one step depends on another. Here it serialises two independent subagents, lengthening runs, and leaves their remits overlapping.

questions.explanation: When parallel subagents duplicate work, partition their scope in the delegation itself: which sources each covers and what each must leave alone. Dynamic subagent selection cuts cost on narrow questions, but it cannot help when every subagent's coverage is genuinely needed.
questions.decider: The affected runs answer broad questions whose reports cite both subagents, so both are needed; if those runs were narrow disclosure questions, sending them to the filings subagent alone would be the better fix.

eli5.question: Two helpers keep doing the same research, and it costs money. The clue is: the reports in those runs use material from both helpers, so both are needed. The cost figure is the loud part. It tempts you to drop a helper.
eli5.answer: Think of two people sent to the same library, one told 'look into competitors' and one 'look into company papers'. Both end up reading the same brochures. The fix is to tell each one which shelves are theirs and which are not (scope partitioning). Both still go, but they stop overlapping. Rule: if two helpers overlap but both are needed, split their territory up front.
options: Runner-up. Sending only the helpers a question needs (dynamic subagent selection) wins for narrow questions. Here both helpers' work ends up in the report.
Correct. Give each helper its own shelves and say which shelves belong to the other.
Removing duplicates at the end (de-duplication) tidies the pile. The double work has already been done and paid for.
Making one helper wait for the other (sequential hand-off) slows the run and still leaves their jobs overlapping.

deep.premise: It is tempting to read a cost complaint as a reason to run fewer subagents. That is right when a question needs only one of them. Here both subagents feed the final report. The waste is that they cover the same ground. Overlap is a boundary problem, fixed by drawing the boundary in the delegation, not by removing a worker.

questions.question: The coordinator's system prompt is a 60-step procedure written around six question shapes: 'Step 1: search the analyst's question. Step 2: extract the companies named…'. On those shapes reports are solid. Last quarter about a third of questions resembled none of the six, and on a question about a pending emissions rule with no named companies, the coordinator worked through the steps into an empty result. Analysts expect the mix of questions to keep widening as new desks adopt the tool. How should the coordinator prompt be rewritten?

options.t: Add a worked decomposition for each question shape, including the emissions case, showing how it was split across subagents.
options.why: Runner-up. Worked decompositions help a coordinator generalise and stay consistent, and they would be the best addition if questions came from a stable, known set. With a third of questions matching none of the shapes and the mix widening, examples tied to past shapes still leave the coordinator copying someone else's steps.

options.t: Keep the procedure and add a branch for questions without named companies that sends them to document analysis first.
options.why: Incorrect. A branch patches the one shape that failed. The next unanticipated shape fails the same way, and the procedure keeps growing.

options.t: Put a classification step at the top that maps each question to the nearest of the six procedures before delegating.
options.why: Incorrect. Mapping a new question to the nearest old procedure still runs steps that do not fit it; the emissions question would get the wrong steps again.

options.t: State the research goal and what a finished report must contain, when evidence is enough and when a return falls short.
options.why: Correct. Coordinator prompts work best as goals plus quality criteria. The coordinator then plans steps for any question shape, and the criteria tell it when the evidence is sufficient or a subagent must be asked again.

questions.explanation: Write coordinator prompts as goals and quality criteria, not step-by-step procedures. Procedures, branches and shape-specific examples all encode the questions someone anticipated; criteria let the coordinator plan for questions nobody anticipated.
questions.decider: About a third of questions match none of the prepared shapes and the mix is widening; if questions came from a small, stable set, worked decompositions for each shape would be the stronger addition.

eli5.question: The coordinator follows a long recipe that fits only six kinds of question. The clue is: a third of last quarter's questions fit none of the six, and the mix keeps growing. So the question is how to brief a coordinator for questions nobody planned for.
eli5.answer: Think of a cook given one recipe card per dish. Ask for a new dish and they are stuck. Tell them instead what a good meal must have, and when a dish is not good enough, and they can plan any dish. That is writing the coordinator prompt as goals plus quality criteria. Rule: brief a coordinator with the goal and the bar it must reach, not the steps.
options: Runner-up. Worked examples (few-shot) help when the menu is fixed and known. Here new dishes keep arriving.
Adding a branch fixes one new dish. The next new one breaks it again.
Picking the nearest recipe (classification) still cooks the wrong dish for a truly new request.
Correct. Say what a good report contains and let the coordinator plan the steps.

deep.premise: It is tempting to think the procedure failed because it was incomplete, so you add branches, examples or a classifier. Each of those still decides the steps in advance for shapes someone foresaw. When a large and growing share of questions are new shapes, the coordinator must plan its own steps against a clear standard: the goal and the quality criteria.

questions.question: An analyst asked about cold-chain logistics capacity in Brazil, Mexico and Chile. The report covered Brazil and Mexico in depth and gave Chile one sentence. The delegation log shows the coordinator created a subtask for each country; the Chile subagent returned two brief findings and noted that most sources it found were Spanish-language trade journals it could only skim. Roughly one report in six ends up lopsided like this. The coordinator then hands the returns to synthesis. Which addition fixes this most economically?

options.t: Have the coordinator check the synthesis draft against the request, re-delegate thin areas, and re-synthesise.
options.why: Correct. The gap appears only after the subagents report back, so the fix is an evaluation step at that point: compare the draft with the request, re-delegate targeted work for what is thin, and re-synthesise. It adds work only to the runs that need it.

options.t: Have the coordinator split each request more finely up front, by country and by market segment, across more subagents.
options.why: Runner-up. A finer decomposition is the fix when the coordinator leaves part of a topic unassigned. Chile had its own subtask, so the gap opened during research, and splitting further raises the cost of every run.

options.t: Have synthesis tag each section with its source count and flag sections under a threshold for the analyst to review.
options.why: Incorrect. Surfacing thin coverage is honest reporting, but it hands the gap to the analyst instead of closing it.

options.t: Have each research subagent repeat its search with broader queries until it returns at least five findings.
options.why: Incorrect. A fixed minimum is an arbitrary threshold. It makes every subagent keep searching, including those whose areas are already covered, and nothing checks whether the report answers the request.

questions.explanation: Coordinators should evaluate the synthesis for gaps, re-delegate targeted subtasks and re-synthesise. Fixing the decomposition helps only when part of the request was never assigned.
questions.decider: The delegation log shows a Chile subtask, so the gap arose from what came back, not from the plan; if Chile had been left out of the decomposition, splitting the request more finely would be the fix.

eli5.question: A three-country report came back nearly silent on one country. The clue is: the coordinator did assign Chile, and the Chile helper came back with very little. So the plan was fine; the follow-up was missing.
eli5.answer: Think of an editor who assigned three reporters. One files a thin story. A good editor reads the draft, spots the gap, and sends that reporter back with a specific ask. That is an iterative refinement loop: check the synthesis for gaps, re-delegate, re-synthesise. It costs extra only on the reports that need it. Rule: if the gap appears after the work comes back, check and re-delegate.
options: Correct. Read the draft against the request and send targeted follow-ups for what is thin.
Runner-up. Splitting the work more finely (broader decomposition) fixes a plan that left a country out. This plan did not.
Labelling thin sections tells the analyst about the gap. It does not close it.
A minimum count makes every helper search longer, even those already done.

deep.premise: It is tempting to blame the decomposition whenever a report misses part of a question, because that is the textbook cause. But a decomposition is too narrow only if something was left unassigned. Here every country had a subtask, and one came back thin. Gaps that appear after research need a check-and-re-delegate loop, not a bigger plan.

questions.question: Spot checks find that 9% of citations in finished reports point at a real, relevant source that does not contain the cited claim. Research subagents return prose paragraphs that mention sources by name in passing. Synthesis merges and rewrites those paragraphs into sections. The report subagent then attaches a URL to each sentence by matching it against every URL gathered in the run. Runs already take 9–16 minutes, and analysts have asked that they get no longer. Which TWO changes together fix attribution?

options.t: Have the report subagent open each cited page and drop or re-match any citation whose page lacks the claim.
options.why: Runner-up. Checking each citation against its page would catch mismatches, and it is a fair safety net when the pipeline cannot change. It adds a fetch per citation to runs that must not get longer, and it detects bad matches instead of carrying the right source through.

options.t: Have research subagents return each finding as fields: claim text, URL, document title and page or section.
options.why: Correct. Attribution is first lost where findings are written as prose. Returning claim and source metadata in separate fields keeps the link as data from the start.

options.t: Give synthesis few-shot examples of merged paragraphs that keep each source's name beside the sentence it supports.
options.why: Incorrect. Few-shot examples improve consistency, but the source names would still live inside prose, and the report subagent would still guess URLs from them.

options.t: Have synthesis pass a claim-to-source list to the report subagent as data, one entry for each claim it keeps.
options.why: Correct. Structured findings help only if synthesis keeps the mapping. Passing claim-source pairs on as data lets the report subagent cite from the mapping instead of matching by similarity.

options.t: Cap each run at its twenty highest-ranked sources and match report sentences against that shorter list.
options.why: Incorrect. Fewer candidates make wrong matches a little less likely, but matching by similarity is still guessing, and the cap cuts research coverage.

questions.explanation: Source attribution survives only if claim-source mappings are kept as structured data from the research subagents through synthesis. Fixing only one end leaves the other to rebuild the link by guesswork.
questions.decider: Runs must get no longer, which rules out checking every citation against its page; with time to spare, verification at the end would be a fair alternative. Both upstream changes are needed because the link is lost twice: in prose findings and again in synthesis.

eli5.question: Citations point to real sources that do not actually say the claim. The clue is: URLs are attached at the very end by matching sentences to a pile of links, and runs must not get any slower. So the question is where the link between a claim and its source gets lost.
eli5.answer: Think of a parcel passing through three depots. If the address label is never attached, or falls off at the middle depot, the last depot has to guess. The fix is a label stuck on from the start (structured claim and source fields) and kept on at every depot (claim-source mapping through synthesis). You need both. Rule: keep claim and source together as data at every step.
options: Runner-up. Checking every citation at the end (verification) catches errors but adds time to every run. It would be fair if time were not capped.
Correct. Attach the label at the start: claim and source as separate fields.
Examples (few-shot) make prose tidier, but the source is still buried in prose.
Correct. Keep the label on through the middle depot: synthesis passes claim-source pairs on.
Fewer links makes the guessing slightly easier. It is still guessing.

deep.premise: It is tempting to fix bad citations where they become visible, at the report step, by checking them. But the link between claim and source was lost much earlier, when findings were written as prose, and lost again when synthesis rewrote them. Provenance has to be carried, not recovered: structured at the source and kept through every hand-off.

questions.question: The synthesis subagent's AgentDefinition was copied from the research template, so it carries WebSearch and WebFetch. In 12% of runs it searches mid-draft, and the passages it pulls in arrive with no claim-source mapping; they account for a disproportionate share of bad citations. A review of 200 of those calls found nearly all were open-ended queries to fill out a sub-topic it judged thin, rather than checks of a single figure. Synthesis is meant to write only from the evidence the coordinator hands it. Which change is most effective?

options.t: Keep its tools and require synthesis to record a claim-source mapping for every passage it retrieves itself.
options.why: Incorrect. Recording provenance for self-retrieved passages would improve those citations, but synthesis would still be doing research outside its role, which the design forbids.

options.t: Swap its search tools for a scoped verify_fact tool for one-figure lookups; route bigger gaps via the coordinator.
options.why: Runner-up. A scoped lookup tool is the right pattern when most of a subagent's extra calls are quick fact checks. These calls are open-ended research to fill a sub-topic, which a one-figure lookup cannot serve and which belongs with the research subagents.

options.t: Take the search and fetch tools out of the synthesis AgentDefinition and have it list unmet gaps in its output.
options.why: Correct. Agents holding tools outside their role tend to use them. Removing search makes the boundary structural, and listing gaps lets the coordinator send them to the research subagents, whose findings carry provenance.

options.t: Add a prompt section to synthesis forbidding new research, with two examples of drafting only from supplied evidence.
options.why: Incorrect. Instructions reduce the behaviour but leave the tools in place, so some out-of-role searching remains; scoping the tool set removes it.

questions.explanation: Give each subagent only the tools its role needs, because off-role tools get used. Scoped cross-role tools fit frequent, simple needs; real research gaps go back through the coordinator.
questions.decider: Nearly all the mid-draft calls are open-ended research rather than single-figure checks; if most were quick checks of one figure, a scoped verify_fact tool would be the better design.

eli5.question: The writing helper keeps doing its own research halfway through writing, and those bits have no sources. The clue is: almost all its searches are open-ended digging, not quick checks of one number. So a small 'check one fact' tool would not cover what it is doing.
eli5.answer: Think of a newspaper. A writer handed research notes should write from them, not run out to report new stories. Take the reporting kit away from the writer (restrict the AgentDefinition's tools) and have them list what is missing, so the editor (the coordinator) can send a reporter. Rule: give each subagent only the tools its job needs; route gaps back through the coordinator.
options: Adding sources to the writer's own digging fixes those citations, but the writer is still doing a reporter's job.
Runner-up. A small 'check one fact' tool (scoped cross-role tool) fits when most calls are quick checks. These are open-ended research.
Correct. Remove the search tools and let the coordinator send gaps to the researchers.
A written ban (prompt instruction) lowers the rate, but the tools are still there to use.

deep.premise: It is tempting to see any cross-role need as a case for a small scoped tool, because that is the textbook answer when a subagent keeps needing one thing from another. It fits only when the need is simple and frequent, like checking one figure. Here the calls are open-ended research. That is the research subagents' job, so take the tools away and send gaps back to the coordinator.

questions.question: Synthesis flagged a contradiction in a report on regional cold storage: one source puts market growth at 12%, another at minus 3%. One is a trade association's annual review; the other is a broker note published this summer that uses trailing-twelve-month figures. Both are reputable, and the analyst reading the draft could not tell which to trust. Each subagent return records a source's title and URL, and nothing else about it. Which change best handles this kind of discrepancy across future reports?

options.t: Have synthesis show both figures side by side, each attributed to its source, and mark the disagreement for the analyst.
options.why: Runner-up. Showing both figures with attribution is right when two sources measure the same thing and disagree. These figures probably cover different periods, so presenting them as a disagreement misinforms the analyst; with no period recorded, synthesis cannot tell.

options.t: Have the fact-check subagent confirm each figure on its source page and drop any figure it cannot locate verbatim.
options.why: Incorrect. Both figures are presumably on their pages; confirming them leaves the apparent contradiction in place.

options.t: Instruct synthesis that when two reputable figures disagree, the more recently published one takes precedence.
options.why: Incorrect. Preferring the newest source picks one figure arbitrarily and discards the other, when both may be right for their own periods.

options.t: Add publication date and period-covered fields to each source record; have synthesis compare periods first.
options.why: Correct. Recording publication and collection dates lets synthesis see that an annual figure and a trailing-twelve-month figure cover different windows, so a timing difference is not reported as a contradiction.

questions.explanation: Require publication and data-collection dates on sources so temporal differences are not read as contradictions. Genuine conflicts over the same period are shown with attribution, not resolved arbitrarily.
questions.decider: One figure comes from an annual review and the other from a trailing-twelve-month broker note, and returns carry no dates; if both figures covered the same period, showing both with attribution would be correct.

eli5.question: Two good sources give opposite growth figures. The clue is: one is a yearly review and the other uses the last twelve months up to this summer. They probably measure different stretches of time, and nothing in the pipeline records which.
eli5.answer: Think of two thermometer readings, one from January and one from July. They disagree, but neither is wrong. You only see that if each reading carries its date. So record when each source was published and what period it covers (publication and collection dates), and compare periods before calling a conflict. Rule: before calling two figures a conflict, check they cover the same time.
options: Runner-up. Showing both with their sources (attributed conflict) is right when both cover the same period. These probably do not.
Checking each figure on its page confirms both are there. The clash remains.
Picking the newest throws away a figure that may be right for its own period.
Correct. Record each source's dates and compare periods first.

deep.premise: It is tempting to treat two reputable figures that disagree as a genuine conflict, and the textbook move for a conflict is to show both with attribution. That move assumes both measure the same thing. Here one is an annual review and one uses a trailing twelve months, so they probably cover different periods. Without dates in the data, synthesis cannot tell a timing difference from a real disagreement.

questions.question: Finance wants the average run cost of $4.10 brought down. Traces show web search and filings analysis opening the same annual report in about 15% of runs. They also show that 60% of questions ask for one figure from one filing, such as a company's reported gross margin, and those runs still pass through all six subagents and produce a full report around the single number. Analysts typically need answers within the hour, while preparing for client calls. Which change will cut cost the most?

options.t: Move research questions to the Message Batches API and deliver each answer to the analyst when its batch completes.
options.why: Incorrect. Batch processing halves cost for latency-tolerant work, but it has no latency guarantee (up to 24 hours) and does not support multi-turn tool calling within a request. Analysts need answers within the hour.

options.t: Let the coordinator gauge what each question needs and spawn only those subagents, sending one-figure lookups to filings.
options.why: Correct. Most questions are single-figure lookups that need one subagent. Selecting subagents by query complexity removes five unneeded stages from 60% of runs, far more than any other option saves.

options.t: Rewrite the search and filings delegations with disjoint source classes, filings to one subagent and press to the other.
options.why: Runner-up. Partitioning scope removes duplicated fetching, and it would be the main lever if overlap drove the cost. It touches about 15% of runs and one subagent's work in them, while 60% of runs carry five stages they do not need.

options.t: Train a routing classifier on past questions that picks one of three fixed pipelines before the coordinator starts.
options.why: Incorrect. A trained classifier with fixed pipelines is heavier machinery than letting the coordinator choose, and it still forces questions into preset shapes.

questions.explanation: Coordinators should select which subagents to invoke by query complexity rather than always running the full pipeline. Fix the largest waste first; duplication between subagents is a smaller, separate lever.
questions.decider: 60% of questions are single-figure lookups that still run all six subagents, against overlap in only 15% of runs; if overlap were widespread and questions mostly broad, partitioning scope would save more.

eli5.question: Research runs cost too much, and two things look wasteful: some duplicate fetching, and simple questions running the whole pipeline. The clue is the numbers: duplicates in 15% of runs, simple one-number questions in 60%.
eli5.answer: Think of a hospital sending every patient through every department, even someone who only needs a blood test. Some departments repeat a test, but the bigger waste is the full tour. The fix is triage: the coordinator sends each question only to the helpers it needs (dynamic subagent selection). Rule: match the pipeline to the question, and fix the biggest waste first.
options: Overnight processing (Batch API) halves the price but can take up to a day. Analysts need answers within the hour.
Correct. Send one-number questions to the one helper that can answer them.
Runner-up. Splitting territory (scope partitioning) fixes the duplicates. It would win if duplicates were the main cost.
A trained sorter with fixed routes (routing classifier) is heavy and still rigid.

deep.premise: It is tempting to go after the waste that is easiest to see: two subagents opening the same report. That is real duplication, and partitioning scope fixes it. But the question asks what cuts cost most, and the bigger waste is quieter: most questions do not need most of the pipeline. Compare the size of each problem before choosing.

questions.question: The fact-check subagent asks the coordinator for more evidence about six times per run, and each round trip adds 30–40 seconds. An engineer proposes letting fact-check invoke the web-search subagent directly. A review of last month's requests found that most were not re-reads of an already cited page but searches for an independent second source, and that in about a third of them the coordinator changed course afterwards, dropping a claim or widening another subagent's brief. Which response is best?

options.t: Keep routing these through the coordinator, as structured asks naming the claim, the sources tried and the gap.
options.why: Correct. Hub-and-spoke keeps routing, error handling and scope decisions in the coordinator, and a third of these requests change its plan. Structuring the request makes each round trip more useful without removing the coordinator from decisions it needs to see.

options.t: Give fact-check a scoped fetch_page tool for re-reading cited URLs, and keep wider searches with the coordinator.
options.why: Runner-up. A scoped tool for the simple, frequent case is the textbook way to cut round trips, and it would win if most requests were re-reads of cited pages. Most are searches for new sources, so it removes few round trips.

options.t: Allow direct subagent calls, logging each one to a shared store the coordinator reads before synthesis begins.
options.why: Incorrect. A shared log tells the coordinator afterwards, but it can no longer redirect the work as it happens, and two subagents now coordinate without it.

options.t: Give fact-check the web-search subagent's tools, letting it gather independent corroborating sources on its own.
options.why: Incorrect. Handing fact-check full search tools over-provisions it and moves research outside its role, and the coordinator still loses sight of requests that change its plan.

questions.explanation: In hub-and-spoke designs the coordinator mediates communication between subagents, so routing, scope and error handling stay in one place. Scoped cross-role tools are for frequent, simple needs; requests that change the plan belong with the coordinator.
questions.decider: Most requests are new searches and a third change the coordinator's plan; if most were re-reads of already cited pages, a scoped fetch tool for that common case would be best.

eli5.question: A checking helper keeps asking the boss for more evidence, and each request costs half a minute. The clue is: most requests are fresh searches, and a third of them make the boss change the plan. So the boss needs to see them.
eli5.answer: Think of a kitchen where the head chef sees every order. If cooks start sending dishes to each other directly, it feels faster, but the head chef stops knowing what is happening. Here a third of the fact-checker's requests change the plan, so the coordinator must stay in the loop (hub-and-spoke). Make the requests clearer instead. Rule: if a request can change the plan, it goes through the coordinator.
options: Correct. Keep the coordinator in the middle and make each request precise.
Runner-up. A small re-read tool (scoped cross-role tool) wins when most asks are simple re-reads. Most here are new searches.
A shared notice board (shared memory) tells the boss afterwards. It cannot steer the work as it happens.
Giving the checker full search tools turns it into a second researcher, outside its role.

deep.premise: It is tempting to see coordinator round trips as pure overhead and remove them. They are overhead only when the coordinator adds nothing. Here a third of the requests make it change course, so they are decisions, not deliveries. Keep them with the coordinator, and save scoped shortcuts for simple, frequent needs.

questions.question: The firm's MCP server over its research library offers search_library, which searches fifteen years of analyst notes by meaning, ranks the hits and returns document metadata. Its description reads 'Search the research library.' The research subagents mostly run Grep over a nightly text export of the library instead and miss notes that use different wording. The same subagents also use Grep on exported price tables, where an exact ticker match is what they want. Which change most reliably redirects library searches?

options.t: Expose the library's folder hierarchy as an MCP resource that subagents browse before choosing notes to open.
options.why: Incorrect. Resources are good for exposing a content catalog and cutting exploratory calls, but browsing folders does not replace finding notes by meaning.

options.t: Remove Grep from the research subagents' allowed tools, leaving the MCP tool as their only search mechanism.
options.why: Runner-up. Removing the competing built-in would redirect every search, and it would win if Grep had no other use for these subagents. They rely on Grep for exact ticker matches in the price tables, so removing it breaks that work.

options.t: Rewrite the tool's text to say what it finds in notes that keyword matching misses, with sample queries.
options.why: Correct. Tool descriptions are the main signal for selection. A one-line description gives the subagents no reason to prefer the MCP tool over Grep; describing what it does that literal search cannot, with sample queries, does.

options.t: Rename search_library to semantic_note_search and leave the one-line text as it stands.
options.why: Incorrect. A clearer name helps a little, but a name alone does not tell the model when the tool beats Grep, and the thin description remains.

questions.explanation: When agents prefer built-in tools over a more capable MCP tool, improve the MCP tool's description so its advantages and use cases are clear. Removing a tool is a blunt fix that also removes its legitimate uses.
questions.decider: The subagents also use Grep legitimately for exact ticker matches on the price tables; if Grep had no other use, removing it would be the more certain redirect.

eli5.question: Helpers keep using a plain word search instead of a smarter library search tool. The clue is: they also use the plain word search on price tables, where exact matches are exactly right. So taking it away would break something.
eli5.answer: Think of a library with a skilled librarian whose desk sign just says 'Help'. Visitors keep using the card index instead. Rewrite the sign to say what the librarian can find that the index cannot (a fuller tool description). Visitors still use the card index for exact titles. Rule: if a better tool is ignored, first make its description say why it is better.
options: A browsable catalogue (MCP resource) helps find where things are. It does not search by meaning.
Runner-up. Taking the word search away forces the switch, but it breaks the exact price-table lookups.
Correct. Make the description say what the tool finds that word search misses.

questions.question: The Sentry error group points at one frame: orders/pricing.py:212, inside apply_regional_discount. The engineer needs every call path that reaches that function and which of those changed in Tuesday's deploy. The orders/ package has 90 files and about 28,000 lines. The session is fresh. Once the paths are known, the engineer will write the fix in this same conversation and wants the callers' actual code in front of Claude while doing it. What is the most effective approach?

options.t: Use Glob for orders/**/*.py and choose the files to open from their names and the directory layout.
options.why: Incorrect. Glob matches file paths, not contents; filenames do not reveal which files call the function.

options.t: Read all 90 files in order, writing a few-line summary of each to a scratchpad file along the way.
options.why: Incorrect. Scratchpad notes help across long sessions, but reading every file up front spends the context on 28,000 lines when a handful matter.

options.t: Delegate the mapping to an Explore subagent with the frame and Tuesday's diff, and work from its summary.
options.why: Runner-up. An Explore subagent isolates verbose discovery and returns a summary, which is right when the main session needs only conclusions or its context is under pressure. Here the session is fresh and the fix needs the callers' code in this conversation, which a summary does not provide.

options.t: Grep for references to the function, Read each hit, then follow those files' imports outward one hop at a time.
options.why: Correct. Grep finds the call sites by content, and reading those files then following imports builds the picture incrementally, leaving the relevant code in the session for the fix.

questions.explanation: Trace code incrementally: Grep for entry points or references, then Read to follow imports, rather than reading everything up front. Use an Explore subagent when the discovery output is verbose and the main session needs only the conclusions.
questions.decider: The engineer will write the fix in this conversation, wants the callers' code at hand, and the session is fresh; if only a summary of paths were needed or context were tight, an Explore subagent would be better.

eli5.question: The engineer needs every route into one function, and will then write the fix right here. The clue is: they want the callers' real code in this conversation while fixing, and the session is fresh. A summary from a helper would leave that code out.
eli5.answer: Think of following a river upstream. You do not map every stream in the country. You start where you care and walk up each branch that feeds it. Here: search for who calls the function (Grep), open those files (Read), then follow their imports. The code you read stays at hand for the fix. Rule: search for the entry point, then read outward step by step.

Runner-up. A helper that explores and reports back (Explore subagent) is right when you need only conclusions. Here the fix needs the code itself.

questions.question: The Sentry MCP server needs an auth token. Sentry's admin issues tokens per person, and the weekly audit attributes every action to the token's owner. Last year a contractor's token leaked through a committed config file, and security has since asked that no credential sits in the repository. The two joiners start Monday; their onboarding checklist is: clone, export your tokens, run Claude Code. Which setup meets these requirements?

options.t: Have each person add the Sentry server to their own ~/.claude.json with their personal token written inline.
options.why: Runner-up. User-level config keeps the token out of the repository and is right for personal or experimental servers. The onboarding checklist expects the server to arrive with the clone, and per-person setup in ~/.claude.json does not.

options.t: Commit the server entry to .mcp.json, with the token field read from ${SENTRY_TOKEN} in each shell.
options.why: Correct. Project-level .mcp.json is shared through version control, and environment-variable expansion lets each person supply their own token without committing it. That fits clone-then-export, the per-person audit and no credentials in git.

options.t: Commit .mcp.json with one read-only team token scoped to the Sentry project, rotated every quarter.
options.why: Incorrect. A shared token breaks per-person attribution in the audit, and committing it puts a credential in the repository.

options.t: Commit .mcp.json with an empty token field and have each person paste their own token in after cloning.
options.why: Incorrect. Typing a real token into a tracked file invites exactly the accidental commit that leaked a token last year.

questions.explanation: Shared MCP servers belong in the project's .mcp.json, with secrets supplied by environment-variable expansion such as ${SENTRY_TOKEN}. User-level ~/.claude.json is for personal or experimental servers.
questions.decider: The onboarding checklist is clone, export tokens, run Claude Code, so the server definition must come with the repository; if the server were a personal experiment, ~/.claude.json would be the right home.

questions.question: For the spike, the engineer gave Claude a fixed plan: read the stack trace, read the failing function, read its callers, check Tuesday's diff, propose a fix. At step three Claude found the function correct; the bad value comes from a serialiser two layers up, whose input changed shape after another team's schema migration. Claude still completed steps four and five and proposed a guard in the failing function. Reviews show about half of this service's incidents start outside it. How should the engineer structure investigations like this?

options.t: Delegate each step of the plan to its own subagent and have a coordinator assemble the five results into a report.
options.why: Incorrect. Separate subagents isolate the work, but the steps are still fixed in advance, and step three's finding still cannot change steps four and five.

options.t: Open each investigation in plan mode and have Claude write the complete step list before it reads any code.
options.why: Incorrect. Plan mode is for designing changes with several valid approaches before editing. An investigation's steps cannot be known before the evidence arrives, so writing the full list first repeats the problem.

options.t: Keep a fixed sequence but extend it with steps for upstream serialisers and recent schema migrations elsewhere.
options.why: Runner-up. A fixed sequence (prompt chaining) works when the steps are predictable, and adding these steps would have covered this incident. With half of incidents starting outside the service, the next one will need steps nobody listed.

options.t: Give Claude the goal and the evidence so far, and let it pick each next step from what the last one found.
options.why: Correct. Debugging is open-ended. Adaptive decomposition generates each subtask from what has been found, so a discovery like step three's redirects the investigation instead of being ignored.

questions.explanation: Use fixed sequential pipelines for predictable, regular work and adaptive decomposition for open-ended investigation, where each step depends on what the last one found.
questions.decider: About half of incidents start outside the service, so the needed steps cannot be predicted; if incidents followed a stable pattern, a fixed sequence extended with the missing checks would serve.

A good detective lets each clue decide the next move (adaptive decomposition). Give Claude the goal and what is known, and let each finding choose the next step. Rule: if what you find changes what you do next, do not fix the steps in advance.
options: Splitting the checklist across helpers (subagents) still fixes the steps in advance.
Planning first (plan mode) is for designing code changes. You cannot plan a hunt before the clues appear.
Runner-up. A longer fixed checklist (prompt chaining) works when cases are predictable. Half of these are not.
Correct. Let each finding decide the next step.

The engineer spawns an Explore subagent to map every route into the order serialiser, with the prompt: 'Investigate the issue we've been discussing and report the call paths involved.' options.why: Correct. Subagents do not inherit the parent's conversation; context must be passed explicitly in the prompt. Without the frame, field and migration, the subagent can only produce a generic survey.

options.why: Incorrect. More tools would let it look things up, but it still would not know which error group, frame or field matters.

options.t: Run /compact before spawning the subagent, and it starts from a condensed copy of the conversation.
options.why: Incorrect. /compact shrinks the parent's context; subagents do not receive the parent's conversation, compacted or not.

evidence.means: A restriction, not a request. That rules out the body instruction in [[3]] and the CLAUDE.md rule in [[0]].

evidence.quote: Whoever runs it usually carries straight on in the same conversation, asking about particular frames and commits it surfaced.
evidence.means: The quiet clue. The detail must stay in this conversation, so a forked skill ([[1]], the runner-up) would leave only a summary.

evidence.quote: Which setup fits best?
evidence.means: Shared, argument-hinted, tool-limited and inline: [[2]].

deep.rule: Fork a workflow when only its summary matters; keep it inline when the user will build on its detail.
